t: The Olmecs built the first great centres of Mesoamerica, San Lorenzo and then La Venta, in the tropical lowlands of Mexico’s Gulf Coast between about 1200 and 400 BCE.
Their sculptors moved basalt blocks of many tonnes from the Tuxtla Mountains to carve colossal heads and thrones, probably portraits and seats of rulers, and worked jade with great skill.
Their images of rulers, gods and the cosmos spread across Mesoamerica and helped shape the art and religion of later peoples such as the Maya, though how far they led that shared culture is debated.
dyk: The Olmecs’ own name is unknown. “Olmec” comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, in which the Olmeca were the “rubber people”, a name for those who lived on the Gulf Coast some two thousand years later.
ev: Offerings, among them the oldest known rubber balls, are laid in the sacred spring of El Manatí
San Lorenzo, above the Coatzacoalcos river, becomes the largest centre in Mesoamerica
San Lorenzo declines, and La Venta in Tabasco becomes the leading Olmec centre
Olmec-style reliefs are carved on the hillside of Chalcatzingo in central Mexico
La Venta is abandoned, and the population of the Olmec heartland falls sharply
Stela C at Tres Zapotes, an Epi-Olmec monument, records one of the earliest Long Count dates
The first known colossal head comes to light at Tres Zapotes, described by José María Melgar y Serrano
Matthew Stirling’s expeditions to Tres Zapotes, La Venta and San Lorenzo begin Olmec archaeology

f.homeland: The tropical lowlands of the Gulf of Mexico in southern Veracruz and western Tabasco, Mexico, with Olmec-style art found from central Mexico and Guerrero to Guatemala and El Salvador
f.period: c. 1200–400 BCE, with roots going back to c. 1600 BCE or earlier; San Lorenzo was the leading centre until c. 900 BCE, then La Venta until c. 400 BCE
f.known: Seventeen colossal stone heads; basalt thrones and other monuments; carved jade and serpentine; the earthen pyramid and buried offerings of La Venta; the oldest known rubber balls
f.sources: Excavations since the 1930s at San Lorenzo, La Venta, Tres Zapotes and El Manatí; their sculpture, offerings and figurines; no deciphered writing; the name itself comes from Aztec accounts of a later people of the Gulf Coast
